item.title: Securitisation 101 — Part 5: Credit Enhancement, Mechanism and Design
item.description: How the model sizes credit enhancement: the credit model, the scenario grid, the cash-flow waterfall, bisection, the sensitivity cushion, the swap and reserve design, and the checks against public deals.

item.title: No Two Banks Say It the Same Way
item.description: The last ten banks through the verification pipeline, read log by log. Why pre-coded Python scraping failed, why checking every cell by hand is not feasible, what it costs in tokens to get a bank through the QA gate, and how the agent's harness evolves session by session. Agents are the only viable path to a curated credit metric database at scale, and without that data a peer credit comparison ranks definitions, not banks.

item.title: Expensive On Purpose
item.description: Verifying one bank's worth of metrics against real source documents cost about half a million tokens. A more efficient reading method barely moved that number. Here's why the cost is the point, not a bug — and why it might belong on a local model instead of a metered API.

item.title: Audit the Neighbor Too
item.description: A metric in active use across 34 banks had never been formally checked. Auditing it properly caught five real bugs. Cross-checking it against the metric next door caught four more, for free.

item.title: Confirmed, Not Claimed
item.description: A field that says a fact is true and a fact that's actually been checked look identical, right up until they disagree. Why file identity now lives in a separate, independently-built register instead of a column on the record it describes.

item.title: Whose Bank Is This?
item.description: Group and subsidiary are both real, both rated, and easy to conflate. Why this project scopes to group-consolidated only, deliberately, with the architecture already built for the alternative it isn't doing yet.

item.title: Post PDF
item.description: A placeholder for the point this whole project is quietly waiting for: machine-readable regulatory disclosure making most of the ingestion layer unnecessary.

item.title: Antidote for Large Liar Model
item.description: Why the ingestion pipeline was designed, from the first line of code, so the LLM writing phase can never become the source of a fact — and what error handling actually means when the failure mode is confident invention, not a crash.

item.title: Not a Specification
item.description: The brief was 'write a bank's credit paper.' That's aspiration, not a specification. This is the outline of what the real problem turned out to be, and the path it set.

item.title: Adding the 61st Bank
item.description: How this project's bank-ingestion pipeline has changed since May, what Claude Code actually does in it now, and what happens end to end when a new bank gets added.

item.title: One Metric, Three Rulebooks
item.description: Why a Stage 3 ratio can't exist on a US bank's balance sheet, and what to do architecturally once you notice a whole class of bug shaped like that.

item.title: WeWork: The Floor Worth More Than the Building
item.description: How a landlord became a tech company, and how one professor's arithmetic exposed the most expensive fiction in recent capital markets history.

item.title: LLM Credit Paper Generator
item.description: Building a domain-grounded AI bank credit analyst — what worked, what didn't, and why fine-tuning was not the answer.

item.title: Securitisation 101 — Part 3: Building the Deal
item.description: From warehouse to tranched deal: pool selection, the frozen static set, rating stresses, capital-stack sizing, a sensitivity cushion, challengers and issuance economics.

item.title: Its Lonely At The Bottom
item.description:
“Never be wrong on your own”

John Maynard Keynes

Except of course that he probably never said it, or if he did it was not recorded as a direct quote. What he did say was below. The motto of Bankers everywhere. We should not be churlish about this, its good advice. In theory the odds of a colossal mistake should diminish with the more eyes looking at the problem. Eventually someone who knows what they are doing should figure out the problem. The challenge here is group think, where the bias rules the day.

item.title: Un consolidating Consolidated Accounting, or a day trip to the Casino
item.description: Accounting tricks to be wary of

item.title: Enron: A Look Back
item.description: Enron did not collapse because of a few bad actors. It collapsed because an entire ecosystem of supposedly intelligent, well-paid professionals chose not to see what was in front of them.
